doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

title: How he became a producer
summary: Phil Woods's accountant-manager producer made far more than the musicians, prompting Goodwin to think he could do it, plus Lester Koenig and Art Pepper at Contemporary.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: So let me talk about, ask you about producing a little bit.
Did you get into it — I’ll just say “on purpose.” How did it occur?

Well it happened because I joined Phil Woods’s band or we joined it was really like a cooperative band. For some reason we played really well together in the original quartet. And Phil had his manager at that time who was also his record producer. And the guy was an accountant and he knew nothing about music. But he’d still tell you how to play. And I had been thinking about it, to say if that guy can do that I could do that gig and I could make ten times what I’m making on this record date, like he is. I was making a hundred bucks, he’d be making a thousand bucks. So I said well I could do better than him.

I wasn’t an audiophile but I really knew how records were made. I’d been hanging out in the studio since I was a teenager and hearing these great musicians and I was no stranger to that part of the business as far as being a musician. But the producer was quite often not really very musically inclined in a way. They were businessmen, I mean they got classic guys, you know the Bob Thiele and the Ertugen brothers and so forth, Lester Koenig was a great model for me from Contemporary Records. And I had befriended him because of my friendship with — or he befriended me because of my friendship with Art Pepper. It was at — I used to go to Contemporary Studios and witness recording sessions. I remember taking Art to a session he was doing with Marty Paich, it was called “The Great Jazz Standards” or something like that, it was about a ten piece band. Wonderful record. Art plays the tenor, alto, and clarinet on it. And Marty’s arrangements — marvelous.
I bet you were soaking it all in.
I was. Soaking it all in, you know like the fly on the wall, a very big fly on the wall.
